# Central tetrahedral section products and two-row capacity faces

These are scoped ordinary/simplex results. Neither is the general mixed-integer conjecture. The first result retains actual section-centroid geometry; the second works for arbitrary probability laws because only two coordinates are involved.

Archive reconciliation: Section 3 below is an independent tetrahedral reproof of a consequence already established in every dimension by `candidate 8704554a92158bfc`, Section 6. The new stronger ingredient here is the specified-captured-vertex cap product bound in Sections 1--2. No novelty is claimed for the central-region depth formula.

## 1. A tetrahedral quadrilateral cap inequality

Let a plane cut a tetrahedron into two parts, strictly capturing vertices 0 and 1 and excluding 2 and 3. Let lambda be the barycentric centroid of the section and let F be the captured volume fraction. Then

    lambda_1<=1/3  implies  F>27 lambda_1 lambda_2 lambda_3.       (1)

The corresponding inequality for captured vertex 1 follows by swapping 0 and 1. Only the other captured vertex's centroid coordinate is bounded in (1).

Here is an exact proof. Parameterize the diagonal intersection by positive homogeneous coordinates x,y,z,w and put S=x+y+z+w. The cutting affine form has vertex values (1/x,1/y,-1/z,-1/w). The cyclic section vertices are

    A=(x,0,z,0)/(x+z), B=(x,0,0,w)/(x+w),
    C=(0,y,0,w)/(y+w), D=(0,y,z,0)/(y+z).

Their diagonal intersection is e=(x,y,z,w)/S. Triangulation along AC gives section centroid (A+B+C+D-e)/3: the two triangle area fractions equal the complementary BD diagonal ratios. Consequently

    3 lambda_1 = y[1/(y+z)+1/(y+w)-1/S],
    3 lambda_2 = z[1/(x+z)+1/(y+z)-1/S],
    3 lambda_3 = w[1/(x+w)+1/(y+w)-1/S].                    (2)

Write P=x+y, R=z+w, a=xy, b=zw and

    D0=(x+z)(x+w)(y+z)(y+w).

The captured volume is

    F=b(PS-a+b)/D0.                                       (3)

For an explicit determinant derivation, use raw vertex heights (p,q,-r,-s). The tetrahedra from vertex 0 to the two section triangles have combined fraction p(alpha+delta), where

    alpha=ps/[(p+r)(p+s)(q+s)],
    delta=qr/[(p+r)(q+s)(q+r)].

The remaining tetrahedron (0,1,C,D) has fraction q^2/[(q+r)(q+s)]. Summing these three determinants and setting (p,q,r,s)=(1/x,1/y,1/z,1/w) gives (3). All denominators are positive, and repeated heights are allowed.

The hypothesis in (1) is exactly

    c=b(S+y)-xy^2>=0.                                    (4)

Define the positive polynomials

    B=R(x+y)+x^2+xy+y^2,
    A=R^3+2R^2 x+3R^2 y+R x^2+5Rxy+3R y^2
                          +2x^2 y+2xy^2+y^3.

Substituting (2)--(3) and clearing positive denominators gives the exact identity

    F-27 lambda_1 lambda_2 lambda_3
      = b[cB+bA+b^2 y]/[S^3(y+z)^2(y+w)^2].             (5)

Every term in the bracket is nonnegative and bA is strictly positive. This proves (1). The identity is polynomial, so (4) is the only sign hypothesis beyond positive diagonal coordinates.

## 2. Other section incidences

For a section isolating one captured vertex r, write its three edge intercepts from r as eta_j, j!=r. The centroid equation is eta_j=3 lambda_j. The cap is a tetrahedron, so

    F=27 product_(j!=r) lambda_j.                         (6)

Intercepts equal to one are permitted; this covers cuts through vertices. For a cap which is the complement of a vertex cap at s, choose any strictly captured vertex r and let j,k be the two remaining labels. Then

    F-27 product_(l!=r) lambda_l
      =1-27 lambda_j lambda_k(lambda_r+lambda_s)
      =1-27 lambda_j lambda_k(1-lambda_j-lambda_k)>=0,     (7)

by AM-GM applied to the three nonnegative numbers lambda_j, lambda_k, and 1-lambda_j-lambda_k, whose sum is one.

A proper plane through an interior point has at least one strictly positive and one strictly negative vertex value. Unless it strictly separates two vertices from two vertices, one of its closed sides is a vertex tetrahedron of the form in (6). Thus (6)--(7) include all remaining incidences, including planes through one or two vertices. No boundary-mass limit is needed: such boundaries have zero tetrahedral volume.

It follows that if every coordinate of the section centroid is at most 1/3, then for every strictly captured vertex r,

    F>=27 product_(j!=r) lambda_j.                        (8)

## 3. Exact ordinary halfspace depth in the central barycentric region

Let b be an interior point of a tetrahedron and suppose its barycentric coordinates satisfy 0<b_j<=1/3. Then its normalized ordinary halfspace depth is exactly

    27 product of the three smallest coordinates of b.   (9)

To prove the lower bound, translate any containing halfspace until its boundary passes through b. A minimum among these cuts exists: the unit-normal sphere is compact and cap volume is continuous because a plane has zero three-dimensional volume. At a minimizing direction the section centroid equals b. Indeed the derivative of cap volume under an arbitrary change of its normal is the section integral of the corresponding linear function of x-b, divided by the normal length. This follows directly by slicing along the normal and dominated convergence; the compact polytope has bounded sections, and the proper section crosses its interior. The vanishing derivatives in all tangent normal directions imply that the section centroid minus b is parallel to the normal. Both points lie in the section plane, so their difference is zero. The same differentiation is valid for a plane through vertices: those boundary faces have zero relative section area and do not affect the integral.

Apply (8) to a strictly captured vertex r of this minimizing cut. Since b_r is at most the largest barycentric coordinate, the product excluding r is at least the product of the three smallest coordinates. This proves the lower bound in (9).

For the upper bound choose a vertex r with largest coordinate. On each incident edge place an intercept eta_j=3b_j<=1. The plane through the three intercepts has section centroid b, because its coordinates at j!=r average to eta_j/3=b_j. Its vertex cap has volume fraction 27 product_(j!=r)b_j by (6), proving equality. This is an ordinary affine-invariant tetrahedron calculation, with no change to a mixed-integer lattice asserted.

## 4. The exact two-coordinate face of D_d

For d>=2, put p=d/(d-1). Recall D_d is the downward set of row geometric means of nonnegative (d+1)-square column-stochastic matrices Y with zero diagonal. A vector with only its first two coordinates possibly positive belongs to D_d exactly when

    v_1^p+v_2^p<=1.                                     (10)

For necessity, the entries Y_12,Y_21 are at most one and every remaining column obeys Y_1j+Y_2j<=1. Thus

    v_1^p <= GM_(d-1)((Y_1j)_(j>=3)),
    v_2^p <= GM_(d-1)((Y_2j)_(j>=3)).

Geometric-mean superadditivity bounds the sum by GM_(d-1)(Y_1j+Y_2j)<=1. Conversely choose theta in [v_1^p,1-v_2^p], set Y_12=Y_21=1, and set Y_1j=theta, Y_2j=1-theta for every j>=3. All other entries are zero. This is an allowed matrix whose two nonzero row geometric means dominate v_1,v_2. The case d=1 is separately D_1=[0,1]^2.

## 5. A universal two-variable probability-capacity bound

Let U,V be nonnegative random variables with U+V<=1 almost surely. Define

    a=inf_(t>0,Pr(U<=t)>0) t/Pr(U<=t)^(1/d),
    b=inf_(t>0,Pr(V<=t)>0) t/Pr(V<=t)^(1/d).

For d>=2 these capacities satisfy a^p+b^p<=1. They are in [0,1] by testing t=1. If either is zero, the conclusion follows immediately. Otherwise their definitions give Pr(U<=t)<=(t/a)^d and Pr(V<=s)<=(s/b)^d for t,s>0, also trivially when a probability is zero.

For every 0<t<1 the events U<=t and V<=1-t cover the probability space. Hence

    1 <= (t/a)^d+((1-t)/b)^d.

The minimum of this expression is (a^p+b^p)^(1-d), attained at t=a^p/(a^p+b^p). This proves the claim. Closed-event overlaps cause no problem: only the union bound is used. No density or non-atomic hypothesis is imposed.

In particular every column-stochastic capacity matrix with at most two nonzero rows has its capacity vector in D_d, in every d>=1. The two row values evaluated on the uniform barycentric simplex sum to one almost surely; all other row capacities are zero. Equations (10) and the preceding probability argument apply. The case of only one row and d=1 follow from the stated separate boundary facts. This does not extend the known three-variable arbitrary-law statement, which is exactly false.
